strengths: The combination of neural operators, adversarial synthetic training distributions, and short Sinkhorn rollouts is a well-motivated contribution to amortized optimal transport. Generalizing a learned initialization across datasets and grid resolutions is practically useful, even though the individual ingredients build on prior work.

The reported empirical improvements are substantial. Table 4 shows approximately 1–3% transport-cost errors across several datasets, considerably outperforming Gaussian initialization and MNIST-trained Meta OT outside MNIST. Cross-dataset experiments, three cost/domain configurations, resolution sweeps, and the marginal-feasibility results in Figures 18–19 provide meaningful supporting evidence. Table 6 also supplies quantitative barycenter results.

Proposition 5 provides a useful fixed-point residual justification for the bootstrapping loss under positive-kernel assumptions. The appendix supplies extensive architectural and training details, links code and model weights, and acknowledges limitations in resolution extrapolation.
weaknesses: The mathematical conventions are inconsistent in ways that affect the connection between theory and implementation. Equation (1) has the wrong sign on KL regularization. More substantively, the dual in Equation (3) uses the reference measure μ⊗ν, so the scaling factors satisfy u_i = μ_i exp(f_i/ε) and v_j = ν_j exp(g_j/ε). Proposition 1 omits these marginal factors, and the network predicts ε log(v). Consequently, Proposition 2 does not directly establish convergence of the learned potentials without an explicit conversion. Algorithm 1 also labels the unregularized transport component ⟨C,Π⟩ as the regularized objective. These quantities and their derivatives need consistent definitions.

The principal generator-universality guarantee does not cover the implemented model. Theorem 3 requires equal input/output dimensions and a Lipschitz constraint, whereas Appendix C uses a 200-dimensional latent vector to generate two 64×64 measures and does not enforce that constraint. This output distribution cannot have the asserted full-dimensional density on the joint simplex. The appendix acknowledges the mismatch but nevertheless concludes that generator coverage cannot bottleneck performance; that conclusion is unsupported.

The downstream optimization formulas contain substantive errors. Algorithm 3 applies softmax directly to probability weights minus a gradient; this is neither simplex projection nor the usual entropic mirror-descent update, and it moves a nonuniform optimum even when its gradient vanishes. Equation (11) omits the derivative of the outer Sinkhorn divergence's source self-interaction term. These formulas must be corrected or reconciled with the implementation before the barycenter and gradient-flow demonstrations establish the claimed geometric behavior.

The evaluation does not isolate the contribution of adversarial training or bootstrapping. Important controls include a fixed synthetic generator, the same predictor trained with the dual objective, and Meta OT trained on comparable synthetic data. Comparing against Meta OT trained only on MNIST demonstrates transfer beyond that particular training distribution, but does not establish that its approach intrinsically cannot generalize. The generator snapshots and qualitative MLP discussion do not replace these controls.

The practical speedup claim needs stronger validation. Table 2 measures time to an oracle threshold of 1% transport-cost error; although marginal-feasibility curves are provided, runtime at matched observable stopping criteria is not. Gaussian initialization lacks a comparable runtime benchmark, and the roughly 35-hour training cost is not accompanied by an amortization analysis. The results support promising acceleration in the tested setting, but the broader state-of-the-art claim remains insufficiently established.
